PercentPlaceholder.definition: The old-style way of putting values into a string: % conversion specifications in the string are replaced by the values to the right of the % operator.

LogToFile.label: Log to file
paras: Logging to a file means sending the log messages to a text file instead of the screen. A file is a named sequence of characters kept on disk, and a text file can be read in any text editor. The chapter passes a filename named argument to basicConfig, as in logging.basicConfig(filename='myProgramLog.txt', level=logging.DEBUG, format=...), and the log messages are saved to myProgramLog.txt (Sweigart, 2025).

Messages on the screen clutter the output of the program and disappear when the window is closed. Written to a file, they keep the screen clear and can be read after the program has run, as the chapter points out (Sweigart, 2025). A file is also the only practical place for the log of a program that runs without anyone watching it.

The option is used when a program runs unattended or writes more messages than anyone would read on a screen, and the file is read afterwards with an editor or a program. The library reference explains the mechanism: specifying filename makes basicConfig create a FileHandler with that name, rather than a StreamHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The file is opened in the mode given by filemode, which defaults to 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and the HOWTO explains the result: if the script is run several times, the messages of successive runs are appended to the file, and a filemode of 'w' makes every run start afresh (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a test in which a short program is run twice with the same file name, the file holds two lines DEBUG - run; run twice again with filemode='w', it holds one.

By default the file grows indefinitely, as the FileHandler documentation warns (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a long-lived program needs a plan for old logs. The HOWTO's file example also passes encoding='utf-8', so that text such as Malmö is written correctly; the glossary explains that a string has to be serialized as a sequence of bytes to be stored, and the text encoding is the rule for that (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And an argument conflict is an error: the library reference says that stream is incompatible with filename, and that giving both raises a ValueError (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
LogToFile.definition: Passing filename to basicConfig sends the messages to a text file instead of the screen.

ForceReconfigure.label: Force reconfigure
paras: Force reconfigure is the option that makes basicConfig replace an existing configuration. The library reference states that the function does nothing if the root logger already has handlers configured, unless the keyword argument force is set to true, in which case the existing handlers are removed and closed before the new configuration is carried out (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The argument was added in Python 3.8.

The rule is a frequent source of confusion, because the second call fails silently. A learner who changes the level in a program, or experiments in an interactive session, sees no effect and no error. Knowing the rule, and the one-word remedy, saves a lot of puzzling.

It is met in the interactive shell, where earlier lines have already configured logging, in test suites, and in programs in which a library configures logging before the main program does. The chapter does not mention the rule.

A program that calls basicConfig with level WARNING and the format 'first %(message)s', then again with level DEBUG and the format 'second %(message)s', and then logs a debug and a warning message prints only first w, because the second call is ignored. After a third call with force=True and the format 'third %(message)s', a debug message prints third d2.

An implicit configuration counts too. The call logging.warning('first') configures the root logger by itself, because it has no handlers, and a later basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is then ignored: a following logging.debug call prints nothing and the level of the root logger is still 30. Place basicConfig before any other logging call, or use force=True when the order cannot be controlled.
ForceReconfigure.definition: basicConfig does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, so a second call is ignored unless force=True is passed.

LoggerObjects.label: Loggers and handlers
paras: Behind the simple module-level functions of logging stands a small system of objects. The Python documentation says that the library takes a modular approach and offers several categories of components: loggers expose the interface that application code uses, handlers send the log records to the right destination, filters decide finer which records to output, and formatters specify the layout of the final output (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The system explains behaviour that the one-line setup hides: why a message from one part of a program can be shown while another is not, why a message can appear twice, and why basicConfig can be ignored. A learner who knows the logger, the handler and the record can read the documentation of logging and the logs of larger programs.

The concepts of this group are the logger, which receives the calls and chooses by level, the handler, which delivers the record to a destination, and the log record, the object that carries the details of one event from the first to the second. Log information is passed between loggers, handlers, filters and formatters in a LogRecord instance (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Logger.label: Logger
paras: A logger is the object on which log calls are made. Each logger has a name, and the names are arranged in a hierarchy by dots, so that the logger 'app.db' is a child of 'app', and all loggers are descendants of the root logger. A logger is always obtained from logging.getLogger(name), and calls with the same name return the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Loggers let the parts of a large program log separately. A name such as the one a module has, which the documentation recommends for the purpose, tells the reader where a message came from, and the threshold of one logger can be changed without touching the others. A library written by someone else can log through its own logger and leave the choices to the application (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the chapter a logger is present but not named: the functions logging.debug, logging.info, logging.warning, logging.error and logging.critical just call the same-named method of the root logger, whose name is printed as root in the output (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Larger programs write logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module, where __name__ is the module's name.

In a check, the call logging.getLogger() returns an object of the class RootLogger whose name is 'root', logging.getLogger('app') is logging.getLogger('app') is True, and once the logger 'app' exists the parent of logging.getLogger('app.db') is the logger named 'app'. A new logger has no level of its own, so its effective level is that of its nearest ancestor with one; for 'app.db' that is the root's level, 30, unless something sets another (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The documentation says that loggers should never be created directly but always through the function getLogger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A message from a named logger is also handled differently when nothing is configured: it is printed as the bare message by the handler of last resort, instead of in the root format. Do not log to the root logger in a library, so that the application can configure it as it likes (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
Logger.definition: The object that receives log calls; the module-level functions use the root logger, and named loggers form a hierarchy by dotted names.

Handler.label: Handler
paras: A handler is the object that delivers a log record to a destination. The logging documentation lists several: a StreamHandler writes to a stream and uses sys.stderr when none is given, a FileHandler writes to a disk file, and there are handlers for email and for system logs, among others (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler also has its own level, which starts as NOTSET so that every record is processed.

Handlers separate what is logged from where it goes. The same record can be sent to the screen and to a file, each with its own format and threshold, without changing the line that logs it. This separation is what makes it possible to change the destination of a whole program by changing its setup only.

In the chapter handlers are created for the reader by basicConfig. Without a filename it makes a StreamHandler, and with filename it makes a FileHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The list of the handlers of the root logger is available as logging.getLogger().handlers: it is the empty list in a program that has not logged anything, and after logging.basicConfig() it holds one handler of the class StreamHandler.

When a logger accepts a call, it creates a record and offers it to its handlers, and then, if its propagate attribute is true, to the handlers of its parent loggers. If no handler is found in the whole chain, the handler of last resort is used, a StreamHandler writing to sys.stderr with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That explains why a warning from an unconfigured named logger still appears on the screen while its info messages do not.

Do not attach the same handler to a logger and to its ancestors: the documentation warns that a record may then be emitted several times (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reason why basicConfig does nothing on a second call is that it checks whether the root logger already has handlers.
Handler.definition: The object that sends a log record to a destination; basicConfig creates a StreamHandler for the screen or, with filename, a FileHandler for a file.

LogRecord.label: Log record
paras: A log record is the object that a logger creates for each event that is logged. It contains all the information pertinent to the event: the name of the logger, the numeric level, the path and line number of the call, the message and the arguments to merge into it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Records are created automatically; the logging reference notes that they can also be made by hand.

The record is the common currency of the logging system. Loggers, handlers, filters and formatters all work on records, and the fields of the record are the names that a format string can use. Knowing what a record holds shows what a log line can contain.

A record is never seen in the simple use of the chapter, but its attributes are what the format string selects: asctime, levelname and message are all attributes of the record (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The attribute levelname is the text of the level, 'INFO' for 20, and levelno is the number.

The message of a record is computed as msg % args when it is needed. With msg equal to 'hello %s' and args equal to ('world',), the call getMessage() returns 'hello world', and the record created for a level of 20 has the levelname 'INFO'. If a message is given without arguments, no percent formatting is done, so the message '100%' is returned as it is (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The record is created only if the logger is enabled for the level of the call, so a call below the threshold is cheap: in a test that counts how many records are created, a debug call to a logger whose threshold is WARNING creates none and a warning call creates one. The formatted message and the time are computed later, when the record is handled. Arbitrary objects can also be used as the message, in which case str is called on them to produce the text (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
LogRecord.definition: The object created for every logging event; it carries the logger name, the level, the message and its arguments, and the place of the call.

Levels.label: Levels
paras: Levels are the importance ranks that log messages carry. There are five of them, from the least to the most important, and each has a name, a number and a function of the same name. The chapter describes them in Table 5-1 and explains that logging levels provide a way to categorise log messages by importance, so that less important messages can be filtered out while testing (Sweigart, 2025).

The levels allow one program to produce a lot of output while it is being developed and little when it is finished, without changing any logging call. The programmer decides the level of each message once, and the setup decides which levels are shown. This turns logging into a dial that can be turned from detailed to silent.

The group has four concepts: the five levels and their numbers, the threshold that selects among them, the default threshold that applies when nothing has been configured, and logging.disable, which silences levels from outside the program's own setup.

LoggingLevels.label: Logging levels
paras: The five logging levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL, in increasing order of importance. Each is a number in the logging module: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, and a sixth value, NOTSET, which is 0, means that no level is set (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter gives the five names with the functions that log at each level: logging.debug(), logging.info(), logging.warning(), logging.error() and logging.critical() (Sweigart, 2025).

A level states how much attention a message deserves. The chapter explains them in its Table 5-1: DEBUG is the lowest level, used for small details that matter only when diagnosing problems; INFO records general events or confirms that the program works; WARNING indicates a potential problem that does not yet stop the program; ERROR records an error that made the program fail to do something; and CRITICAL is the highest level, for a fatal error that has caused, or is about to cause, the program to stop (Sweigart, 2025).

Each level is used by calling the function with the same name as the level in lower case. A program that sets the level to DEBUG with format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' and logs one message at each level prints DEBUG - d, INFO - i, WARNING - w, ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c, in the order of the calls.

The numbers make the comparison of importance possible: a message is accepted if its number is not lower than the threshold. The module defines the five names as constants, so logging.DEBUG is the number 10 and logging.CRITICAL is 50. Levels of one's own can be defined with logging.addLevelName, but all levels used must be registered with it, and the documentation calls a custom level higher than CRITICAL not recommended (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The level of a message is the programmer's judgment, not a property that Python can check: as the chapter says, it is up to you to decide which category your log message falls into (Sweigart, 2025). Do not use CRITICAL for routine trouble, since a level that is used for everything no longer separates anything.
LoggingLevels.definition: The five levels run from lowest to highest importance, and each has a number: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50.

LevelThreshold.label: Level threshold
paras: The level threshold is the level below which messages are ignored. It is set with the level argument of basicConfig, and a logger set to a threshold accepts messages of that level and above. The documentation of setLevel says that messages less severe than the level will be ignored, and messages of that severity or higher are emitted, unless a handler's own level is higher (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The threshold is the dial of the chapter's logging system. During development it is DEBUG, which the chapter says shows messages from all the logging levels. Later, when the programmer is interested only in errors, level=logging.ERROR shows only ERROR and CRITICAL messages and skips the DEBUG, INFO and WARNING messages (Sweigart, 2025).

It is set once, in the setup of the program, and often read from a setting so that a user can ask for more detail without editing the program. The HOWTO shows how to turn a command-line option such as --log=INFO into the number to pass as level, with getattr(logging, loglevel.upper()) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In a program that sets level=logging.ERROR and logs one message at each level, only ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c appear. The comparison uses the numbers: 40 and 50 are not lower than the threshold 40, whereas 10, 20 and 30 are. Nothing is deleted or changed in the logging calls; changing the one word in the setup brings the other messages back.

There are two thresholds, one in the logger and one in each handler, and a message must pass both. The logger's level is checked first; a handler with a higher level of its own will drop the record afterwards. If a message does not appear although the logger's level is low enough, look at the level of the handler.
LevelThreshold.definition: A message is shown only if its level is at least the threshold, so raising the threshold hides the lower levels without deleting any call.

DefaultLevel.label: Default level
paras: The default level is the threshold that applies when the program has not configured logging. The documentation states that the default level is WARNING, which means that only events of this severity and higher are tracked unless the logging package is configured to do otherwise, and that the root logger is created with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The default explains a very common surprise. A learner writes logging.debug('value is 3') and sees nothing, because debug messages are below the default threshold. The chapter avoids the surprise by always calling basicConfig with level=logging.DEBUG first (Sweigart, 2025).

The default is met in any program that imports logging and logs without a setup, in the interactive shell, and in code that libraries run. In such a program logging.warning('Watch out!') prints WARNING:root:Watch out!, and logging.info('I told you so') prints nothing, as the HOWTO shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The expression logging.getLogger().getEffectiveLevel() evaluates to 30 in a fresh program, the number of WARNING. The functions logging.warning and logging.error find no handler on the root logger, and so they call basicConfig themselves, with the default format, to the error stream; a program that calls logging.warning('w') and logging.error('e') prints WARNING:root:w and ERROR:root:e. A named logger that has no configuration at all is served by the handler of last resort, which prints the bare message, such as bare, for WARNING and above (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The side effect on the root logger is the trap: after the first implicit call the root logger has a handler, so a later basicConfig is ignored. Debug messages that are missing from the output are therefore explained by the default threshold or by an earlier implicit configuration, and the fix is level=logging.DEBUG in a first call of basicConfig or force=True.
DefaultLevel.definition: Without basicConfig the threshold is WARNING, so debug and info calls print nothing and warning and error calls print to standard error.

DisablingLogging.label: Disabling logging
paras: Disabling logging means switching log messages off from one place, without deleting the calls. The function logging.disable(level) provides an overriding level for all loggers, which takes precedence over each logger's own level, and its effect is to disable all logging calls of severity level and below (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's recipe is logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL), which suppresses all log messages (Sweigart, 2025).

A finished program should not fill the screen with debugging messages, and deleting the calls would make the next debugging session start from nothing. A single line that can be commented out or in turns all the messages on and off. The chapter advises putting it near the import logging line so that it is easy to find (Sweigart, 2025).

It is used at the end of development, in tests that should run quietly, and in a program that wants a global quiet switch. Called with no argument, it uses the level CRITICAL, which is the default since Python 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In a program that sets level=logging.INFO, logs a critical message, calls logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) and logs again, the first message appears as CRITICAL - before and the later critical and error messages are silent. Calling logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) removes the override, so a following error message appears as ERROR - after. A call with logging.INFO discards INFO and DEBUG events only, so a later warning still prints.

The disable level applies to all loggers in the process, including those of libraries, and it overrides their own settings, so a program that disables logging for a test must undo it. The setting is a number: logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) is the way back, not logging.enable, which does not exist.
DisablingLogging.definition: logging.disable silences the given level and all below it; disabling CRITICAL turns every message off, and NOTSET turns them back on.

Practice.label: Practice
paras: Practice in logging is the set of habits that decide whether log messages help or hinder. The first habit is to choose logging and not print for the diagnostic output of a program, and the second is to write the log calls so that they cost little when the messages are not wanted.

A log that is easy to switch off, and cheap when off, is a log the programmer will leave in the program. A log full of expensive string building is one that has to be removed before the program is released, which brings back the problem that logging was meant to solve.

The two concepts are the comparison of logging with print, which the chapter makes in its section A Poor Practice and in its practice questions, and the lazy formatting of messages, which the logging documentation explains.

LoggingVersusPrint.label: Logging versus print
paras: Logging and print both write text, but they serve different readers. The chapter's rule is that log messages are intended for the programmer, not the user, and that for error messages the user should see, like File not found or Invalid input, please enter a number, a print call is the right tool (Sweigart, 2025). The practice question that asks why logging messages are better than print calls for the same message has the answer in the same section.

The chapter calls debugging with print a poor practice. When the debugging is done, the programmer has to remove each print call, and may accidentally remove calls that were used for non-log messages. With logging, a program may be filled with as many messages as the programmer likes and all of them can be disabled later with one logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) call (Sweigart, 2025).

The Python logging HOWTO sets the same division in a table: to display console output for the ordinary usage of a command line script or program, use print; to report events that occur during normal operation, such as for status monitoring or fault investigation, use a logger's info or debug method (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Each log call also adds a level and, if the format asks for it, a time, and it goes by default to the error stream, whereas print goes to the standard output. A program that prints one line with print and logs one line with logging.warning shows both until logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) is called; after it only the print line remains.

The distinction is easy to blur in small scripts: a message the user needs, such as the result of the calculation, must be printed, and must not depend on the logging setup, or it would vanish when logging is disabled. The chapter's factorial program makes the point: print(factorial(5)) is part of the original program, so the code displays the result even if logging messages are disabled (Sweigart, 2025).
LoggingVersusPrint.definition: Log messages are for the programmer and print is for the user; log calls stay in the program and one setting switches them all off, where print calls would each have to be deleted.

LazyFormatting.label: Lazy formatting
paras: Lazy formatting means that the text of a log message is built only if the message is actually going to be emitted. A call such as log.debug('value is %s', obj) hands the message and the argument separately to the logger; the HOWTO says that formatting of message arguments is deferred until it cannot be avoided (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An f-string, by contrast, builds the whole text before the call is made.

Building a message can be costly, for example when an object has a long text form, and a program that logs inside a loop may build thousands of messages that no one will read. With deferred formatting a disabled debug call costs little more than the call itself, which makes it affordable to leave such calls in a finished program.

The form is common in the code of libraries and of larger applications, which pass the values after the message as in log.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total). The percent markers are the ones explained under percent placeholders.

A small experiment shows the difference. A class is a recipe for objects, and the method __str__ is what Python calls to turn an object into text; here it counts its calls. With the level at INFO, log.debug('value is %s', obj) leaves the count at 0, log.debug(f'value is {obj}') raises it to 1 although nothing is printed, and log.info('value is %s', obj) raises it to 2 and prints INFO:demo:value is noisy.

Lazy formatting defers only the formatting. The arguments themselves are evaluated before the call, so an expensive function call among them still runs. The HOWTO's advice is to guard such a call with if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG), so that the expensive functions are never called when the logger's threshold is above DEBUG (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
LazyFormatting.definition: A message given arguments is formatted only when it is emitted, so a disabled debug call costs no string conversion, unlike an f-string built before the call.

Debugger.label: Debugger
paras: The debugger is a tool that runs a program one instruction at a time and lets the programmer look at the program between the steps. The chapter defines it as a feature of the Mu editor that executes a program one instruction at a time, giving a chance to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). A program started this way is said to run under the debugger. The same idea is offered by IDLE, by other editor software, and by the module pdb, the Python debugger, which ships with Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The debugger shows what a program actually does instead of what its author thinks it does. The chapter admits that the process is much slower than running the program at full speed, but it lets the programmer see the actual values in a program while it runs, rather than deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Exceptions, assertions and logging must be written into the program before it runs, and a question that the programmer did not think of in advance cannot be answered by them. The debugger can be started without changing the program, and then any variable can be read at any point.

The chapter teaches the debugger inside the Mu editor, with buttons and a pane at the side of the window. The same tool is found in IDLE, whose documentation lists a debugger with persistent breakpoints and stepping among its features, and in the module pdb, which is part of the standard library and is controlled by typing short commands at a prompt (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in function breakpoint() lets a program start the debugger by itself at a chosen line, and since Python 3.14 pdb can also attach to a program that is already running.

The branch has three groups. The first, the debugger interface, describes what the person sees: the editor, the act of running under the debugger, the pane that lists the variables, and the button that stops the session. The second, the controls, describes how the person moves through the program: breakpoints, Continue, Step In, Step Over and Step Out. The third, the Python debugger, shows the same controls as commands of pdb and explains breakpoint(), the environment variable that configures it, and attaching to a running process.

The debugger shows only the values that the program has at the moment it is paused. It does not remember how the values got there, so a bug whose cause lies far back in the run can still require several sessions or a log. The chapter also reminds the reader that a program that waits for typed input still waits under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Finally, the debugger is a convenience of the editor or of pdb and not a feature of the language, so the buttons and wording of one tool do not carry over unchanged to another.

DebuggerInterface.label: Debugger interface
paras: The debugger interface is everything the person at the keyboard sees and touches while a program runs under the debugger. The chapter describes it for the Mu editor: the editor window in which the debugger is started, the Debug button that starts it, the Debug Inspector pane that lists the values of the variables, and the Stop button that ends the session (Sweigart, 2025). These four parts are the subject of the concepts in this group.

The same four parts exist in every debugger, even though their look differs. IDLE starts its debugger from a toggle in a menu and marks breakpoints through a context menu (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and pdb replaces buttons and panes with commands typed at a prompt and answers printed as text. A student who knows what each part is for can therefore use whichever tool is at hand, and can read a transcript of a debugging session without having the window in front of them.

The concepts follow the order of a debugging session: the editor in which it takes place, running a program under the debugger so that it pauses before its first line, reading the program state in the inspector pane, and stopping the program. The controls that move the program forward, namely breakpoints, Continue and the three kinds of step, belong to the next group. Because the windows of Mu cannot be reproduced in text, the transcripts quoted in this group were produced by running pdb on the same kind of program.

MuEditor.label: Mu editor
paras: Mu is the code editor that the chapter uses for its programs. An editor is a program for writing source code, and Mu adds to it the means to run a program and to run it under the debugger. The chapter says that the debugger is a feature of the Mu editor, IDLE, and other editor software (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the top row of buttons has a Run button and, next to it, a Debug button, and the file being edited is shown in a file editor with a number for each line.

A named editor gives the instructions of the chapter something to refer to. The chapter's instructions say to click a button or to click a line number, and they are only understandable if the reader knows which window and which button are meant. The editor is also where the program's text, its output and its debugger meet: the program is edited in the file editor, a running program writes into the output pane, and, as the chapter notes, a program that calls input() waits for the answer to be typed into that output pane (Sweigart, 2025).

The window of Mu appears in the figures of the chapter. Figure 5-1 shows the program paused before its first line, with that line highlighted in the file editor, and Figure 5-3 shows the pane at the right with the variables of the adding program (Sweigart, 2025). Other editors offer the same facilities under other names. The IDLE page of the Python documentation, for example, describes a Debugger entry that makes code entered in the Shell or run from an Editor run under the debugger, and IDLE is described in the glossary as an editor and interpreter environment that ships with the standard distribution of Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Starting the debugger in Mu is a matter of clicking Debug instead of Run. The Debug Inspector pane then opens at the right side of the window, and Debugging mode adds the buttons Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out to the top of the editor, next to the usual Stop button (Sweigart, 2025). Everything else, editing the text and saving the file, works as before. The same program can therefore be run in the two ways one after the other, which is how the chapter proceeds with its adding program.

Mu is one editor among many, and its buttons and menus are not part of Python. The chapter itself remarks that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025), a convenience that a command-line debugger does not necessarily share. The IDLE documentation warns that its debugger is still incomplete and somewhat experimental (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a button named in the chapter is not found in another editor, the underlying idea, pause, look, step, continue, is what to search for.
MuEditor.example: the Mu window with a Debug button next to Run
MuEditor.definition: The code editor used in the chapter; it has a Run button, a Debug button and a Debug Inspector pane, and its output pane is where a running program receives typed input.

RunUnderDebugger.label: Running under the debugger
paras: Running a program under the debugger means starting it through the debugger instead of running it directly. The program does not run to its end at once. It is paused just before its first line of code and waits for the programmer to say what to do next. In Mu the Debug button, next to the Run button, starts this mode, and the first line, the one about to be executed, is highlighted in the file editor (Sweigart, 2025).

A normal run gives no chance to look inside: the program starts, prints its output and ends, and the programmer sees only the result. Under the debugger the programmer gets control before the first line and after every step, which is the only way to watch a variable change from line to line. The price, in the chapter's words, is speed: the process is much slower than running the program at full speed (Sweigart, 2025). The mode is therefore used on a program that is already known to misbehave, such as the adding program that prints 5342.

The command-line debugger is started with the command python -m pdb followed by the name of the file. The documentation says that, as with a script, the debugger pauses execution just before the first line of a module started this way (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript the program starts with a line def double(x): and the first thing the debugger prints is > main.py(1)<module>() followed by -> def double(x):. The first line names the file and the line number in parentheses, with <module> standing for the top level of the file, outside any function, and the second line shows the instruction that is about to run.

The debugger then prints its prompt, (Pdb), and waits for a command. After the command n, which executes the current line and pauses at the next one in the same function, the next stop is on line 4, val = 3, because lines 2 and 3 belong to the function that line 1 only defines; after another n the stop is on line 5, result = double(val). Lines 2 and 3 run only when the function is called. This shows that the debugger moves through the lines in the order in which they execute, not the order in which they are written.

Running under the debugger changes nothing about what the program does, only when it does it, so effects such as printing, asking for input, or writing a file all still happen. If the program ends, pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted and stops again before the first line, as the executed run of the coin program shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And ending the session with the quit command aborts the program being executed, so lines after the stopping point never run.
RunUnderDebugger.definition: Running a program under the debugger starts it paused just before its first line, so that the programmer decides how it goes on from there.

ProgramState.label: Program state
paras: The state of a program is what the program holds at one moment: the values of its variables and the position of the line that is about to run. The chapter describes the debugger as a way to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). Each executed line can change the state, so a running program is a sequence of states, and the debugger lets the programmer stop the sequence and look at one of them.

A bug is a state that is not the one the programmer expected, and a wrong state always comes from some line. The chapter contrasts seeing the actual values in a program while it runs with having to deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Deduction can be wrong in exactly the places where the bug hides, whereas the state seen in the debugger is the real one. The skill of debugging is largely the skill of comparing the state that is shown with the state that was expected.

The chapter's coin program is a good example of state. After 500 of the 1,000 flips, the variable i holds 500 and the variable heads holds the number of heads so far, which the programmer wanted to read at the halfway point (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript, a breakpoint on the line print('Halfway done!') followed by the command c stops there, and p i prints 500. The state also includes which line comes next, which pdb shows with an arrow after each stop.

The state changes with every step. In the executed transcript of a two-line program that assigns x = 1 and then prints x, the command p x on line 1 prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined, because the line that creates x has not run yet; after the command n, p x prints 1. In a loop the state changes on every pass: with a breakpoint on the if line of the coin program, the first c stops with i equal to 1 and the second with i equal to 2.

The state is only what is true now. A pause shows the value that a variable has at that moment and not the values it had before, so a wrong value found at a pause may have been created many steps earlier. The programmer then has to run again with an earlier breakpoint, or step through the earlier lines while watching the value. A state that looks right also proves little, since the bug may show itself only with other values.
ProgramState.example: heads is 500 at the halfway point
ProgramState.definition: The state of a program at a moment is the values of its variables together with the line that is about to run; the debugger shows both.

InspectorPane.label: Debug Inspector pane
paras: The Debug Inspector pane is the part of the Mu window that lists the current value of each variable of the program. It opens at the right side of the window when the program is run under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Each row names a variable and shows the value that it has at this moment. When the program is paused, the pane is a snapshot of the variables, and it changes whenever the program moves on.

The pane is where the debugger answers the question that logging and assertions can only answer in advance: what is in the variables now. In the chapter's adding program, the pane shows that the variables first, second and third hold the string values '5', '3' and '42' instead of the integer values 5, 3 and 42, and that is the whole bug (Sweigart, 2025). The quote marks around the values are the evidence. Without them the pane would show 5, 3 and 42 and the problem would stay hidden.

In Mu the pane is shown beside the file editor throughout a debugging session, as in Figure 5-3 of the chapter. In pdb the same information is requested on demand with the command p followed by an expression, which prints the value of the expression in the current context (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that assigns first = '5', second = '3' and third = '42', the command p first prints '5' with its quote marks, and p first + second + third prints '5342'.

The pane lets the programmer test a theory before changing anything. In the adding program the theory is that adding the three variables joins their text, and the evidence is the quote marks. The cure follows from it: int() turns each string into a number, and in the executed transcript p int(first) + int(second) + int(third) prints 50. In pdb the command p can take any expression, so the same session can answer many questions about the state of the program without editing the file.

The pane shows values, but a value alone can mislead. The text '5' and the number 5 look alike unless the display shows the quote marks,. Also, the pane shows the program as it is when paused and says nothing about how it got there, so the programmer should step through the preceding lines while watching the value change. In pdb, asking for a variable that has not been assigned yet prints an error line that says the name is not defined.
InspectorPane.example: first, second and third shown as strings
InspectorPane.definition: The pane at the right of the Mu window that lists the current value of each variable of the paused program.

StopControl.label: Stop button
paras: The Stop button ends a debugging session immediately. The chapter says that to stop debugging entirely, without bothering to execute the rest of the program, one clicks the Stop button, and that it immediately terminates the program (Sweigart, 2025). It is the usual Stop button of the editor, which is also available during debugging, next to the buttons that Debugging mode adds (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the equivalent is the quit command, which the documentation says aborts the program being executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A debugging session can end before the program does, at the moment the answer is found. A student who has seen in the pane that a variable holds a string has no need to run the remaining lines, and may not want them to run at all if they would write a file or wait for further input. Stop is the control that says the session is over and the program should not go on, whereas Continue says the program should go on without the debugger's pauses.

In Mu the button is on the top row of the editor. In pdb the command is q or quit, and an end-of-file on the input has the same effect (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that prints a line called end after its last statement, giving the command q at the first stop prints nothing of the program at all, because it never reached the print, and the output ends with the (Pdb) prompt. In 3.14 the documentation adds that a confirmation prompt is shown if the debugger was invoked in inline mode, which is the mode that breakpoint() uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The two ways of leaving a session differ in what happens to the rest of the program. Continue runs the rest of the program at full speed, stopping only at breakpoints (Sweigart, 2025). Stop terminates it. With pdb there is a third case, in which the program reaches its end by itself: pdb then reports that the program finished and will be restarted and returns to the first line, ready for another run (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Stopping is not the same as finishing. A program stopped in the middle may have printed only part of its output, written only part of a file, or changed things that the rest of the program would have changed back. And stopping the debugger does not remove the bug: the programmer still has to edit the program and run it again.
StopControl.definition: The Stop button ends the debugging session at once and terminates the program without running its remaining lines.

Controls.label: Controls
paras: The controls are the means by which the programmer moves a paused program forward, or tells it where to pause. The chapter lists the buttons that Debugging mode adds to the editor: Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out (Sweigart, 2025). The fifth control is the breakpoint, a mark on a line that makes the program pause whenever it gets there. Every control answers the question of how far the program should run before it stops again.

A debugger is only as useful as the control the programmer has over it. Stepping through a long program one line at a time takes too long, and running it at full speed lets the interesting moment go by. The chapter shows how the controls divide the work: breakpoints and Continue skip the part of the program that is not of interest, and the steps examine the part that is. The chapter notes, for instance, that stepping through the 1,000 flips of its coin program would take thousands of clicks (Sweigart, 2025).

The controls are the buttons at the top of the Mu window, the entries of IDLE's debugger window, and the commands of pdb. The documentation of pdb names them step, next, return, continue and break, each also available in the short form s, n, r, c and b (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's questions at the end ask for exactly these differences between the three step buttons and for the moment at which Continue stops.

The concepts come in this order: the breakpoint, which places a pause in the program, Continue, which runs to the next pause, and the three steps, which move by a line, over a call, or out of a function. For each control the text gives the button of Mu, the command of pdb, and an executed transcript on a small program in which a function named double is defined on line 1 and called on line 5.

Breakpoint.label: Breakpoint
paras: A breakpoint is a mark on a line of code that makes the debugger pause whenever the program reaches that line. The chapter says that setting a breakpoint on a specific line forces the debugger to pause whenever the program execution reaches that line (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the breakpoint is set by clicking the line number in the file editor, which makes a red dot appear next to the number, and it is removed by clicking the line number again (Sweigart, 2025).

Breakpoints solve the problem of speed. Stepping through the program with the debugger is helpful but can also be slow (Sweigart, 2025), and often the interesting moment is far from the start. The chapter's coin program flips a coin 1,000 times, and the question of interest is the value of heads at the halfway point, when 500 flips are done. With a breakpoint the program runs at full speed to that moment and stops there, where the clicking of Step Over thousands of times would otherwise be needed.

In the chapter the breakpoint is placed on the line print('Halfway done!'), inside the if statement that checks whether i is 500. In the executed transcript of that program, the pdb command b 7 sets a breakpoint on line 7 and prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:7; the command c then runs the loop and stops at line 7, and the command p i prints 500 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation describes break as setting a break at a given line number in the current file. IDLE has the same facility through a context menu and, as its documentation says, saves the breakpoints of a file in the user's .idlerc directory (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The line matters. The chapter points out that a breakpoint on the if statement itself would stop at every pass through the loop, because that line runs on every iteration, whereas a breakpoint on the line inside the if stops only when the execution enters the if clause (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript a breakpoint on line 4, the if line, followed by two c commands, stops with i equal to 2, so each pass stopped once. After a stop the programmer can use Continue, Step Over, Step In or Step Out as normal (Sweigart, 2025).

A breakpoint on a line that never runs never stops the program, and a breakpoint on a line that runs very often stops very often. In IDLE, the documentation says that breakpoints only have an effect when running under the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a program started with the plain Run command ignores them. In IDLE the breakpoints of a file are kept in the .idlerc directory and not in the program file, so the saved program is unchanged. A line that holds no instruction cannot carry a breakpoint: in the executed transcript, b 5 on a blank line prints *** Blank or comment and sets nothing, while b 4 on the line before it prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:4.
Breakpoint.example: a red dot at a line number
Breakpoint.definition: A breakpoint marks a line at which the debugger pauses the running program so its variables can be read.

ContinueControl.label: Continue control
paras: Continue is the control that lets a paused program run at normal speed again. The chapter says that clicking Continue causes the program to execute normally until it terminates or reaches a breakpoint, and that someone who is done debugging and wants the program to go on normally should click it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is continue, or c, and the documentation says it continues execution and stops only when a breakpoint is encountered (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Continue is the control that joins the two modes of work. Between breakpoints the programmer wants the program at full speed, and at a breakpoint the programmer wants it slowly. Without Continue, a debugging session would have to choose one or the other. With it, a session reads like a story: the program starts paused, Continue runs it up to the breakpoint, the programmer looks and steps, and Continue runs it up to the next one.

In the chapter's coin program the program starts in a paused state at the first line, as usual, and clicking Continue makes it run at full speed until it reaches the line with the breakpoint (Sweigart, 2025). The executed transcript shows the same: after b 7 the command c ends with the stop at line 7, with the 500 flips behind it. If a second c is given, there is no further breakpoint, so the program runs on, prints its last lines, and pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted.

Continue stops for one of two reasons only: a breakpoint or the end of the program. If the same breakpoint is inside a loop, Continue stops again on every pass, and in the executed transcript of the breakpoint on the if line, the first c stopped at the first pass and the second c at the second. The chapter's last review question asks when the debugger stops after Continue, and the answer is just these two cases (Sweigart, 2025).

Continue is not Stop. It leaves the debugger attached, and a breakpoint that is later reached pauses the program again, while Stop ends the session. And Continue offers no protection against a program that never ends: a loop that never finishes runs forever under Continue if no breakpoint is hit. In that case the programmer must interrupt the program or use the Stop button.
ContinueControl.definition: Continue runs the program until the next breakpoint or the end.

StepIn.label: Step in
paras: Step In is the control that executes the next line and then pauses again. The chapter adds that if the next line is a function call, the debugger steps into that function, jumping to the function's first line of code (Sweigart, 2025). The pdb command for the same control is step, or s, and the documentation says it executes the current line and stops at the first possible occasion, either in a function that is called or on the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The control is for looking inside. When the value that arrives from a function call is wrong, the cause is either the arguments or the function, and Step In is how the programmer enters the function to find out which. It gives the finest view of a program, one line at a time through every call. The finest view is also the slowest, and the chapter therefore says that Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025).

In the executed transcript of the program that defines double on line 1 and calls it on line 5, the stops are line 1, line 4 and line 5. At line 5 the command s prints --Call-- and then > main.py(1)double() with -> def double(x):, so the debugger has entered the function and shows the name of the function in the place where <module> stood before. The word Call is how pdb marks a stop caused by entering a function.

Step In behaves differently depending on the line. On a line that is not a call, it does the same as Step Over: it executes the line and pauses at the next. On a line that calls a function written in the program, it enters. The chapter notes that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of pdb on a program whose lines 1 and 2 call print(), the command s on line 1 prints a and stops on line 2, so it did not enter print().

Step In on the wrong line leads into code that does not matter. The chapter warns about this with its adding program: the reader should use Step Over instead of Step In on the line that calls print(), because there is no interest in the code of print() (Sweigart, 2025). And once inside a function, the programmer must remember to get out again, with Step Out, or continue stepping through the lines of the function until it returns.
StepIn.definition: Step In executes the next line and, if that line is a call, pauses on the first line of the called function.

StepOver.label: Step over
paras: Step Over is the control that executes the next line of code like Step In does, but treats a function call as a single step. The chapter says that, if the next line calls a function, Step Over steps over, or rushes through, the code in the function: its code runs at full speed and the debugger pauses as soon as the call returns (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is next, or n, and the documentation says that the difference between next and step is that step stops inside a called function, while next executes called functions at nearly full speed, stopping only at the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Most of the time the programmer knows which functions work and wants to follow the main line of the program. The chapter's example is a call of a function named spam() whose inside does not matter: Step Over runs it and pauses when it returns, and the chapter concludes that for this reason Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025). The control keeps the session short and the attention on the code under suspicion.

In the adding program, the chapter uses Step Over for each of the print() and input() calls, from line 1 to the final print() on line 7, since stepping into the built-in functions would be pointless (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of the program with the function double, three n commands go from line 1 to line 4, to line 5 and to line 6, and after that the command p result prints 6. The call on line 5 ran completely in the third step, and the debugger never showed a stop inside the function.

The control is a decision about detail. By choosing Step Over on a line, the programmer says that the result of the line matters but how it was computed does not. If the result later turns out to be wrong, the programmer can start again, or use the breakpoint, and choose Step In on that line. The stops of the debugger stay in the same function, the one that is being examined, and each stop is the next line of that function.

Step Over hides what happens inside the call, including a bug. A function that has a mistake can return a wrong value, and Step Over will report only that the line finished. If an exception is raised inside the call, it is still raised: in the executed transcript, the command n on a line that calls a function whose body divides by zero prints ZeroDivisionError: division by zero and stays on the calling line. And when a line waits for typed input, the chapter notes that the highlighting goes away while Mu waits for the text (Sweigart, 2025).
StepOver.definition: Step Over executes the next line as a whole, running a called function without pausing inside it.

StepOut.label: Step out
paras: Step Out is the control that runs the rest of the current function at full speed. The chapter says that it causes the debugger to execute lines of code at full speed until it returns from the current function, and that it is meant for the reader who has stepped into a function call with Step In and now simply wants to keep executing instructions until leaving it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is return, or r, and the documentation says it continues execution until the current function returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The control repairs a step that went too deep. After Step In the programmer is on the first line of a function. If it turns out that the function is not under suspicion, walking through every one of its lines is a waste, and Step Out spends them at full speed. It is the counterpart of Step In in the way that going back is the counterpart of going forward, and it is used less than Step Over because a careful programmer steps in only where it is wanted.

In the executed transcript, the command s at line 5 enters the function double and stops on its first line, and the command r then prints --Return-- followed by > main.py(3)double()->6 and -> return y. The arrow and the number after it show that the function is about to return the value 6. The debugger has stopped on the return line, one step before control passes back to the caller, and one more step with n would continue in the calling code.

Step Out is therefore a way of saying finish this function. It does not skip the lines that follow in the caller. A breakpoint on a line of the function that has not yet run still stops the program first: in the executed transcript a breakpoint is set on line 2 of double after stepping into it, and the command r then stops on line 2 and not at the return. After the stop at the return, pdb shows the value that the function returns after the arrow, so the programmer can see the result before it is used.

Step Out from the top level, outside any function, has no function to leave. In the executed transcript the command r on line 1 of the program runs everything, so 6 and end are printed, and the stop is on the last line, where pdb prints --Return-- with ->None. The tools also differ in where they pause: the chapter speaks of executing at full speed until the function is left, and pdb pauses on the return line itself. The reader who needs the stop to be in the caller should take one more step.
StepOut.definition: Step Out runs the rest of the current function at full speed until it returns.

PythonDebugger.label: Python debugger
paras: The Python debugger is the debugger that comes with Python itself, the module pdb. The documentation says that pdb defines an interactive source code debugger for Python programs, with breakpoints, single stepping at the level of source lines, source code listing, and evaluation of Python code in the context of the paused program; it also supports post-mortem debugging, which means examining a program after it has crashed, and can be called under program control (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's controls all exist in it as commands.

Unlike the buttons of an editor, pdb belongs to the standard library, so it comes with Python. It needs no window: the executed transcripts of this chapter were produced by starting it as a separate program and typing its commands as lines of input. It can be started in three ways: from the command line with python -m pdb followed by the file name, from inside the program by the function breakpoint(), and, since Python 3.14, by attaching to a process that is already running. The concepts below take the ways in turn.

The module is met whenever a Python program is run with python -m pdb, and whenever breakpoint() is reached. Its prompt is (Pdb). The documentation also shows the case of a program that has crashed: pdb.pm() can be called afterwards to enter the debugger at the place where the exception occurred and to print the value of a variable there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Started as a module, pdb enters this post-mortem mode automatically if the program exits abnormally; in the executed transcript of a program that divides by zero on its second line, pdb prints Uncaught exception. Entering post mortem debugging and stops on that line.

The concepts of this group begin with the two ideas that the later ones depend on: the process, which is a running program, and the environment variable, a named setting handed to a program when it starts. They continue with the function breakpoint() and the hook that it calls, with the commands of pdb that correspond to the buttons of the chapter, and with attaching to a running process, which is new in Python 3.14.

Process.label: Process
paras: A process is a program that is running. PEP 768 speaks of running Python processes and of attaching to a live process by process ID (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The number that identifies a process is its process identifier, abbreviated PID, and the function os.getpid() returns the current process id (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The abbreviation appears in the options of pdb, where the documentation speaks of attaching to the process with the specified PID.

The idea matters for debugging because running programs can be pointed at by number. A debugger that is started together with a program controls that one program. A debugger that attaches to a program that is already running needs to know which one, and the process identifier is the answer.

The process identifier is met in the command python -m pdb -p 1234 and in the call sys.remote_exec(1234, script) of Python 3.14 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed expression isinstance(os.getpid(), int) evaluates to True, and os.getpid() > 0 does too.

Two runs of Python are two processes even if they run the same file. The documentation of the subprocess module says that it allows a program to spawn new processes (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a process spawned in this way has an identifier of its own: in the executed check, the number printed by the child differs from the number of the parent. A process also has an environment, which is the subject of the next concept.

The identifier belongs to one run only, since two runs are two processes. A tool that is pointed at a wrong number would examine another program, so the number should be read from the program itself, for example by printing os.getpid(), at the time it is needed.
Process.definition: A process is a running program as the operating system sees it; each process has its own identifier, which os.getpid() returns.

EnvironmentVariable.label: Environment variable
paras: An environment variable is a named piece of text that belongs to the environment in which a process runs. It belongs to the process environment, which the program can read. The documentation of the os module describes os.environ as a mapping object whose keys and values are strings that represent the process environment, with the example that environ['HOME'] is the path of the home directory on some platforms (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The glossary defines a mapping as a container object that supports arbitrary key lookups, and a dictionary is one (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Environment variables let a user change how a program behaves without editing it. For debugging this is valuable: the same program file can be run with its breakpoints active on one day and switched off on the next, and the file does not change. Python's own settings use the same means. The variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT, which is the subject of the following concepts, decides what the function breakpoint() does.

In os.environ, the executed expression type(os.environ).__name__ evaluates to '_Environ', the class that holds the environment. A program reads a variable with os.environ.get('NAME'), which gives None when the variable is not set; the executed check prints None for a name that is not set. The documentation also says that the mapping may be used to modify the environment, and the executed check shows that a variable assigned in os.environ is visible to a child process that is started afterwards (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The documentation says that the mapping is captured the first time the os module is imported, typically during Python startup, and that changes made to the environment after this time are not reflected in os.environ, except for changes made by modifying os.environ directly (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that changes os.environ changes the environment that it passes on: in the executed check the parent sets GREETING to hi and the child that is started next prints hi, while 'GREETING' in os.environ is True in the parent.

Values are text. The documentation says that keys and values are strings, so a setting such as 0 is the string '0', not the number zero (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It adds that on Windows the keys are converted to upper case, so a name written in lower case is stored in upper case there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And a program that wants a value must handle its absence: os.environ.get('NAME') returns None when the variable is not set, but os.environ['NAME'] has no such default.
EnvironmentVariable.definition: A named text setting that the operating system hands to a process when it starts; Python reads it through os.environ.

BreakpointFunction.label: Breakpoint function
paras: The built-in function breakpoint() puts a breakpoint into the program itself. Writing breakpoint() on a line makes the program stop in the debugger when it reaches that line. The documentation of pdb says that, called with defaults, it can be used instead of import pdb; pdb.set_trace() (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 553, which proposed the function, describes it as a new built-in that enters a Python debugger at the call site (Warsaw, 2017).

PEP 553 lists the disadvantages of the older idiom: it is a lot to type (27 characters), it is easy to mistype, and it ties debugging directly to the choice of pdb (Warsaw, 2017). The new function is short, and because it does not name pdb, the debugger that it starts can be chosen without changing the program. The PEP adds that even where an editor has a user interface for setting breakpoints, it may still be more convenient to just edit the code (Warsaw, 2017).

The function is used in scripts, and the pdb page of the documentation shows an example in which breakpoint() is the first line of a function double, followed by a session in which p x prints 3 and continue lets the program finish (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run of a small program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and then prints after, the output contains before, then a (Pdb) prompt, and, after the command c, the word after.

The function does little itself. It calls sys.breakpointhook(), passing on whatever arguments it received, and returns what the hook returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The default hook starts pdb at the line after the call. The function therefore behaves as the hook decides, which the next concept explains. The executed expression sys.breakpointhook.__name__ evaluates to 'breakpointhook', the default hook that breakpoint() calls.

A breakpoint() that is left in the program will stop it for whoever runs it, including users who have no one to type commands. It should be removed before the program is shared, or switched off with the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, for which the executed run prints before and then the program went on without any pause. The documentation also says that if sys.breakpointhook cannot be reached, breakpoint() raises RuntimeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And since the default hook starts pdb.set_trace(), which expects no arguments, calling breakpoint(1) raises a TypeError, as the executed check shows.
BreakpointFunction.definition: The built-in breakpoint() pauses the program in the debugger at that line; it calls sys.breakpointhook, and PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 makes it do nothing.

BreakpointHook.label: Breakpoint hook
paras: The breakpoint hook is the function that breakpoint() calls: sys.breakpointhook. A hook is a name that holds a function which other code calls, so replacing the function changes what happens. The documentation says that by default the hook drops the programmer into the pdb debugger, but it can be set to any other function so that a different debugger is used (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This is the design of PEP 553, which proposed the hook and the environment variable together (Warsaw, 2017).

A hook lets one line of code, breakpoint(), serve many debuggers. A programmer who prefers another debugger can set the hook once, and the programs need not change. The environment variable also lets the person who runs the program turn the call off. The default hook consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT: if it is set to 0, the hook returns at once and does nothing; if it is not set or is empty, pdb.set_trace() is called; otherwise the variable names a function to call, in the dotted form package.module.function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The executed runs show each case. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, a program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and prints the program went on shows no pause. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to builtins.print, breakpoint('hello', 'hook') prints hello hook, because the named function receives the arguments that were passed. And a program that assigns its own function to sys.breakpointhook has that function called, with its arguments, and breakpoint() returns what the function returns.

The environment variable is read each time the default hook is called. If it names something that cannot be imported, the documentation says a RuntimeWarning is reported and the breakpoint is ignored (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to no.such.module.func, the error output ends with RuntimeWarning: Ignoring unimportable $PYTHONBREAKPOINT: "no.such.module.func", and the program carries on, printing went on.

A program that replaces sys.breakpointhook by its own function no longer consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT, as the documentation says; in the executed run the replaced hook still ran with the variable set to 0 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And the setting 0 silences only breakpoint(): in the executed transcript, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, the command b 2 inside pdb still stops the program on line 2.
BreakpointHook.definition: The function sys.breakpointhook is what breakpoint() calls; by default it starts pdb, but the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT or a replacement function can change it.

PdbCommands.label: Pdb commands
paras: The commands of pdb are the text form of the controls of the chapter. At the prompt (Pdb) the programmer types a command and presses Enter. The commands that correspond to the buttons are step (Step In), next (Step Over), return (Step Out), continue (Continue) and break (Breakpoint), and the command quit corresponds to the Stop button (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each also has a short form, s, n, r, c, b and q.

The commands make the controls of the chapter available in a terminal and in scripts, and they add to them. The command p expression evaluates an expression in the current context and prints its value, so it does the work of the Debug Inspector pane. The command where prints a stack trace with the most recent frame at the bottom and an arrow marking the current frame, which is the call stack of Chapter 4 viewed from the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command list shows 11 lines of source code around the current line, with -> marking the current line (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the executed transcripts every control of the chapter appears as a command: n and s give the stops on lines 4 and 5 and then --Call-- at the start of double; r gives --Return-- and the value 6; b 6 prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:6, and c stops there, where p result prints 6. The check on the class Pdb confirms that the six methods do_step, do_next, do_return, do_continue, do_break and do_where exist, which is the evaluated io example of this concept.

The commands steer the paused program, and a statement written after an exclamation point is executed in its context; the point can be omitted unless the first word of the statement resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation says that print() can also be used, but it is not a debugger command and executes the Python print() function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command-line form python -m pdb [-c command] file starts the program paused at the first line, and -c runs commands as if they were in a .pdbrc file (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A name that matches a command is read as the command: the documentation says the exclamation point can be omitted only unless the first word resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript a variable called c holds 5, and p c prints 5, whereas typing c alone is the command continue and the program ran on to its end. Before a variable has been assigned, p prints an error line: p x on line 1 of a program that assigns x on that line prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined.
PdbCommands.example: step, next, return, continue, break, where
PdbCommands.definition: The standard debugger pdb offers the chapter's controls as commands: step, next, return, continue and break, and where lists the call stack.
io: [c for c in ('do_step','do_next','do_return','do_continue','do_break','do_where') if hasattr(__import__('pdb').Pdb, c)]

RemoteAttach.label: Remote attach
paras: Remote attach is the ability of the debugger to join a program that is already running. Since Python 3.14 the command python -m pdb -p 1234 attaches to the process with that PID (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It rests on the function sys.remote_exec(pid, script), which executes a file of Python code in the process with the given identifier (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and on PEP 768, which proposed a safe external debugger interface for CPython (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024).

PEP 768 states the need: developers often need to analyze application behavior without stopping or restarting services, which is especially crucial for high-availability systems, and very few Python tools could attach to running processes (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The What's New page for 3.14 calls the new interface a crucial capability for high-availability systems and production environments, since tools can inspect and interact with Python applications in real time (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The interface is used by debuggers and other tools, and the documented command is python -m pdb -p followed by the number of the process. The function sys.remote_exec is available on Unix and Windows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed demonstration starts a child program that prints ready and then sleeps; the parent calls sys.remote_exec on its identifier with a script that prints injected, and the child's output then contains injected. On a Python older than 3.14 the function does not exist, so there is nothing to call.

The function returns at once, and the code is run by the main thread of the target process at the next available opportunity; there is no interface to learn when it ran, and the caller must keep the file in place until it has (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The target must run the same major and minor version of CPython as the caller (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation of pdb adds that a process blocked in a system call or waiting for I/O attaches only once the next bytecode instruction is executed, and the glossary defines bytecode as the internal representation of a Python program in the CPython interpreter (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The same power is a risk, since a tool that can run code in another process could be misused, so the feature can be disabled: with the environment variable PYTHON_DISABLE_REMOTE_DEBUG, with the option -X disable-remote-debug, or at build time with --without-remote-debug (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It also needs the same version on both sides. The runnable example of this concept is deliberately small: it checks only that sys.breakpointhook is callable, because attaching needs a second running process of the same version and cannot be shown in one expression.
RemoteAttach.definition: Since Python 3.14 the debugger can attach to a running process by its identifier, using sys.remote_exec.

ModernPractice.label: Modern practice
paras: Modern practice is the part of the chapter in which the four instruments, exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are used together on programs that contain real mistakes. The chapter does this three times. It repairs a factorial function with the help of log messages, it finds why an adding program prints a wrong sum with the help of the debugger, and it ends with a practice program, a coin toss guessing game that the author says has multiple bugs in it, to be found by running the program a few times (Sweigart, 2025). The word modern points to the tools of current Python, which the other branches describe one by one.

Knowing what an instrument does is not yet knowing when to use it. A learner who has read about the debugger still has to decide, faced with a program that prints the wrong number, whether to print values, to add a check or to step through the lines. The practice cases give that decision a concrete setting. The chapter's own advice is that, in general, the earlier you catch bugs, the easier they will be to fix (Sweigart, 2025), and a worked case shows what catching a bug early looks like in a real program.

The cases are met in the chapter's three programs and in the programs a learner writes afterwards. A loop that starts at the wrong number, a running total that begins with the wrong value, input that arrives as text instead of numbers, a random number that is compared with a word, and a test of membership applied to the wrong kind of value all appear in programs of a few lines. Each of these has a name in this branch and a short executed example.

The branch has one group, the worked cases. Each case names a kind of mistake, shows the symptom that it produces, shows the evidence that exposes it and states the repair. The first two cases, the off-by-one range and the starting value of an accumulator, belong to the factorial. The third, string concatenation, belongs to the adding program. The last three, the random integer, the membership test and the type mismatch comparison, belong to the coin toss game. The cases are exercises in reading evidence, and the evidence is always a value that is not the one expected.

A case is a pattern and not a recipe.
